name: The AI Equity Project: AI for Impact Challenge and Community AI Workshops
title: The AI Equity Project: AI for Impact Challenge and Community AI Workshops
answer: The AI Equity Project is a nonprofit running the AI for Impact Challenge, described as the world's first student competition focused solely on applying AI for good, alongside free workshops where elders and teens build AI projects together. Its most useful contribution is a concrete alternative to benchmark-driven contests: teams interview a community group, design an AI solution for its needs, and are judged on creativity, impact, clarity, community relevance and usability rather than dataset size or model choice.

sections.body: The AI Equity Project publishes this site, which covers its two main programmes: the AI for Impact Challenge (AIIC) 2025, a student competition, and a series of free hands-on AI workshops. The pages read include the about page, the AIIC competition pages, the entry requirements page, the workshops page and the chapters page. The material is organisational and programme documentation rather than research, and the competition is dated 2025.
sections.heading: What this source is

sections.body: The AI for Impact Challenge is presented as the world's first student competition focused solely on applying AI for good. Teams must be affiliated with a registered chapter, and no experience or funding is required. Each entry addresses the 2025 challenge question, how AI can help people better access the information, resources or services they need most. Participants identify a community group affected by the year's global problem, interview them about their challenges and needs, and design an AI solution tailored to that problem with feedback from those they aim to help. Entries include an intro video, a proposal completed with a template and feedback from an AI professional, a four-page report or a video of three minutes or more, a prototype or MVP, and impact evidence. Submissions are judged holistically on creativity, impact, clarity of explanation, community relevance and usability. Top teams are paired with university labs and mentors to refine, scale or patent their idea. The workshops page describes free sessions in which elders and teen volunteers explore AI together, producing digital keepsakes, personal assistants for reminders and daily tasks, podcast episodes, recipe preservation, adaptive puzzles and learning plans. The about page explains the project was created because students from underrepresented or under-resourced backgrounds are shut out of AI, and that most competitions reward tools, datasets or compute over ideas.
sections.heading: What it says

sections.body: The source states that over 20 participants created digital keepsakes in one workshop, over 40 participants created personalized assistants in a workshop on building a personal AI assistant, over 30 participants created digital keepsakes in a workshop on family stories and recipes, and over 20 participants created digital keepsakes in each of the thinking and learning-coach workshops. It says no prior tech experience is needed for the thinking and learning-coach workshops. It defines the 2025 challenge question and lists five judging criteria: creativity, impact, clarity of explanation, community relevance and usability. It states that participants do not need to train a model to win.
sections.heading: Figures and claims worth noting

sections.body: For readers following AI in nonprofits, this source shows a working model of community-centred AI education and competition. It documents how a nonprofit structures youth and elder participation, requires teams to interview affected community groups before designing anything, and judges solutions on community relevance and usability rather than model performance. The workshop descriptions give concrete examples of low-barrier AI uses for older adults, from reminders and meal planning to recipe preservation, which nonprofits considering digital inclusion programmes can compare against their own offerings.
sections.heading: What it means for AI in Nonprofits

sections.body: The material is promotional and programme-specific. It gives no independent evaluation of the workshops or competition, no cost data, and no evidence beyond participant counts. The competition pages are dated 2025 and the chapters page lists local chapters without further detail. The site does not address nonprofit operations, fundraising or sector-wide AI adoption.
